analysis.investment_thesis: KPI Green Energy is a fast-growing Indian IPP riding India's renewable energy buildout, compounding revenue at 93% over 6 years — but it is a capital-consumption machine, not a capital-generation machine, with FCF of -₹1,297 Cr in FY25 and ROIC of ~9%, well below my 15% hurdle. The business is growing impressively but has yet to prove it can earn adequate returns on the ever-growing capital it devours.
key_strengths: Explosive, consistent revenue growth (93% CAGR 6Y: ₹34 Cr → ₹1,735 Cr) with expanding operating margins (30.6%).
India's renewable policy tailwind (500 GW target) provides a long, visible project runway — real secular demand.
Promoter skin-in-the-game at 49.5%; ROE of 19.7% and ROCE of 17.5% remain respectable given asset build-out phase.
key_risks: Chronic FCF destruction: FCF negative every year (-₹1,297 Cr in FY25), entirely dependent on equity raises and debt to fund growth — a treadmill that punishes shareholders if capital markets close.
Leverage risk: Borrowings surged to ₹2,533 Cr in FY25 (Debt/EBITDA ~4.4x, above my 2.5x comfort ceiling) on an EBITDA of ₹575 Cr — highly interest-rate sensitive.
ROIC of ~9% (NOPAT/Invested Capital) is structurally below cost of capital, meaning scale alone doesn't solve the economics unless project returns improve.
red_flags: Equity base tripled in one year (₹836 Cr → ₹2,650 Cr in FY25), implying a massive dilutive equity raise — per-share value creation is diluted even as absolute profits grew.
OCF/Net Income = 64% (₹208 Cr OCF vs ₹325 Cr net profit) — below the 80% earnings quality threshold; profits are not converting to cash.
CWIP jumped to ₹709 Cr — significant execution and cost-overrun risk sitting on the balance sheet.
analysis.detailed_analysis:
KPI Green Energy is a genuine growth story in Indian renewables, but through Munger's lens it fails the most important test: it does not generate free cash flow. Every rupee of profit is overwhelmed by capex (₹1,505 Cr in FY25 alone), requiring the company to continuously tap equity and debt markets to survive. Borrowings have grown from ₹139 Cr in FY20 to ₹2,533 Cr in FY25 — a 18x increase — while Debt/EBITDA stands at ~4.4x. This is not a franchise; it is an infrastructure accumulator whose returns depend on project-level IRRs that are structurally capped by power purchase agreement tariffs. ROIC of ~9% is below any reasonable cost of capital in India today.

The inversion test is damning: what happens if interest rates stay elevated, if state DISCOMs delay payments (a chronic Indian utility problem), or if the equity market loses appetite for renewable paper? The entire growth engine stalls or reverses. That said, the operating economics are improving (finance costs fell from ₹86 Cr to ₹79 Cr despite rising debt, suggesting refinancing gains), and India's clean energy buildout is among the most durable secular themes globally. At P/E 20.6x and EV/EBITDA 14.3x, the valuation is not egregious for the growth rate — but I require businesses that generate cash, not consume it. This is a speculative growth bet dressed as a value stock. Hold if already owned; don't initiate at this capital return profile.
